lesson.title: The Bell Curve Emerges: The Central Limit Theorem
lesson.summary: The Central Limit Theorem states that for a large enough sample size, the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the population it was drawn from.
lesson.body:
Every result so far in this unit describes the center and the spread of the sampling distribution of x-bar: its mean is mu, and its standard deviation is sigma divided by the square root of n. Neither of those facts says anything about the shape of the distribution, whether it is symmetric, skewed, bell-shaped, or something stranger. The Central Limit Theorem fills that gap, and it is one of the most remarkable results in all of statistics.

The Central Limit Theorem states that as the sample size n grows large, the sampling distribution of x-bar becomes approximately normal, no matter what shape the original population distribution has. The population itself might be heavily right-skewed, like household income, or oddly bimodal, or even uniform, and it does not matter: averages of large enough samples from that population will still trace out a distribution that looks close to a normal curve. If the original population happens to already be normal, then x-bar is exactly normal for every sample size, even n as small as 2. The theorem's real power shows up when the population is not normal, since it still guarantees approximate normality once n is large enough.

How large is large enough depends on how far the population departs from normal. A population that is only mildly skewed with no serious outliers may look approximately normal in its sampling distribution of x-bar with a sample size as small as 15 or 20. A population that is heavily skewed or has extreme outliers typically needs a larger sample, often n of 30 or more, before the normal approximation becomes trustworthy. This n of 30 figure is a widely used guideline in introductory statistics, not a strict cutoff, and the underlying justification always comes back to how non-normal the original population is.

Here is a worked example showing why this matters practically. Suppose a population of household repair costs is right-skewed, with population mean mu = 50 dollars and population standard deviation sigma = 20 dollars. If you tried to compute probabilities about a single repair cost using a normal curve, you would get poor answers, since individual costs are not normally distributed. But suppose we take a sample of n = 64 repairs and look at x-bar, the sample mean cost. First, the standard deviation of x-bar is sigma divided by the square root of n, which is 20 divided by the square root of 64, or 20 divided by 8, which equals 2.5. Because n = 64 is comfortably large, the Central Limit Theorem tells us the sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal with mean 50 and standard deviation 2.5, even though individual repair costs are skewed. To find the probability that a sample of 64 repairs has a mean cost above 52.5 dollars, compute a z-score: z = (52.5 - 50) / 2.5 = 2.5 / 2.5 = 1.0. Using the standard normal distribution, the proportion of area above z = 1.0 is about 0.1587, so there is roughly a 15.9 percent chance that a random sample of 64 repairs has an average cost above 52.5 dollars.

This is the payoff for the entire unit. The sample proportion and the sample mean are both unbiased, and both have standard deviations that shrink predictably as sample size grows, but the Central Limit Theorem is what lets us actually calculate probabilities about them using the normal distribution, turning the abstract idea of a sampling distribution into a tool that answers concrete questions, as long as the sample size is large enough and the earlier conditions in this unit are met.
